syllabus.clause: PostgreSQL's page layout as the reference: a fixed-size page with a header, line pointers, tuples, free space and a special area. A self-describing format carries a magic number, format version, slot info, a checksum (CRC32C) and the page LSN. Encode endianness and alignment explicitly (→ Ch.5).

at.step: Measured: an untouched page's own checksum validates cleanly, and a single corrupted byte anywhere in its body genuinely invalidates that same checksum
Measured: the checksum, recomputed over the new bytes, still validated cleanly; only checking the magic number itself caught that the format had changed
Measured: the same raw bytes, read in the chosen byte order, gave back the exact original value; read in the opposite byte order, they genuinely gave back a different value

at.step: The same documentation also says something stronger about an item identifier's own index inside a page: it's never moved until freed, so it can be used to reference an item on a long-term basis, even while the item itself moves around during compaction. That's the whole reason a slot and a physical offset are two different things

items.item: The checksum field itself is zeroed before computing the checksum over the rest of the page, an explicit struct-layout choice matching how a real self-describing page would avoid the checksum covering its own stored value; this is why recomputing the checksum after changing the magic number still produces a checksum that validates against itself.

at.step: Now instead of corrupting a byte, change the page's own magic number to something else, and recompute the checksum over those new bytes. Does the checksum alone catch that the format itself has changed?

items.item: The crate used for the checksum (crc32c) is deliberately chosen over the more commonly reached-for crc32fast crate, since crc32fast implements the plain CRC-32 IEEE polynomial, not the CRC-32-Castagnoli algorithm the syllabus names explicitly; the two produce different checksum values over identical bytes.

items.item: The byte-order measurement reads the exact same in-memory byte array two different ways rather than writing it out twice in two different orders, isolating the claim to the reading side alone: the same bytes genuinely mean two different numbers depending only on how they are interpreted.
